\chapter{I Am, You Are}
\label{ch:sein}
\hlchaptermodality{16}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say what someone is in German, using any of the six present forms of the verb for “to be” — and say that I am tired.}

sein is the one German verb whose forms cannot be guessed from its infinitive, so this chapter meets them one at a time — bin, bist, ist, sind, seid, sind — and only assembles the grid once every cell has had its own lesson. It closes with müde, the adjective that finishes ich bin, and a short exchange that runs on nothing but this verb.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[sein]{sein — \textquotedblleft{}to be\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:GE-C16-sein}



\begin{quote}
You have met the German verb for \emph{to have}. Here is its partner — the most irregular verb in German, and the one verb whose forms you will not be able to guess.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: sein}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{sein} — \textquotedblleft{}to be.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

The \textbf{-en} on the end is the infinitive ending you already own from \emph{gehen} and \emph{sehen}: the dictionary form of a German verb wears it, and \emph{sein} wears it too.

That is where the resemblance stops. \emph{Gehen} and \emph{sehen} keep their stem in every form — \emph{ich gehe}, \emph{ich sehe}. \emph{Sein} keeps nothing. Not one of its present forms contains the letters \emph{s-e-i-n} in that order.

This is the only verb in the book that has to be met one form at a time, and the next several lessons do exactly that: one form each, said until it is automatic, before any of them are ever seen side by side.

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{s-voiced} — a German \textbf{s} before a vowel buzzes like English \textbf{z}, exactly as it does in \emph{sehen}. So \emph{sein} opens with a \emph{z}.
  \item \texttt{diphthong-ei} — German \textbf{ei} is the vowel of English \emph{eye}, never \textquotedblleft{}ee\textquotedblright{}.
  \item \texttt{final-t} — worth having ready now, because two of the forms coming up end in a crisp, fully released \textbf{t}.
\end{itemize}

Put together, \emph{sein} sounds like English \textbf{zine}.
\end{sounds}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}sein\textquotedblright{} (\emph{zine}) — buzzing \emph{z}, \emph{ei} as in \emph{eye}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}gehen, sehen, sein\textquotedblright{} — three infinitives, one ending
  \item \textquotedblleft{}sein — to be\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}sein, sein — \emph{zine}.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{sein} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}\textbf{To be}.\textquotedblright{}) Which ending does it share with \emph{gehen} and \emph{sehen}? (\textbf{-en}, the infinitive.) How does the \emph{s} sound? (Like English \textbf{z}.) And the \emph{ei}? (Like English \textbf{eye}.) Next: the first form, and it looks nothing like the word you just learned.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ich bin]{ich bin — \textquotedblleft{}I am\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:GE-C16-ich-bin}



\begin{quote}
You have \emph{ich}, and you have the infinitive \emph{sein}. Put them together and you get a form that shares no letters with either half of that sentence except the \emph{i}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: ich bin}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{ich bin} — \textquotedblleft{}I am.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

One syllable, short \emph{i}, ordinary \emph{b}, ordinary \emph{n}. There is no rule behind it and nothing to derive it from: \emph{bin} is simply the form that goes with \emph{ich}, and it is learned the way you learned \emph{hallo}.

It rhymes with English \emph{bin}, and that rhyme is not an accident — see below.

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{ich-laut} — \emph{ich} still ends in the soft breathy sound you met when you first said \textquotedblleft{}I\textquotedblright{}: tongue where it sits for \emph{ee}, air pushed past it, no scrape.
  \item \texttt{i-short} — the \emph{i} of \emph{bin} is short and clipped, the vowel of English \emph{bin}, not the long \emph{ee} of \emph{ihm}.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{Bin} rhymes with English \emph{be} for a reason, even though the vowels have drifted apart. Both come from Proto-Indo-European \textbf{*\emph{b\textsuperscript{h}uH-}} — \textquotedblleft{}to grow, to become.\textquotedblright{}

So German kept that ancient root in the \textbf{present tense} and English kept it as the \textbf{infinitive}: \emph{be} and \emph{bin} are the same old word wearing different jobs. Hold on to that; two lessons from now it explains something about the whole verb.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}ich bin\textquotedblright{} — short \emph{i}, soft ending on \emph{ich}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}ich bin Anna.\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}ich bin Peter.\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}bin — be\textquotedblright{} — the same old root
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}ich bin, ich bin.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}I am.\textquotedblright{} (\textbf{Ich bin}.) Is the \emph{i} of \emph{bin} long or short? (\textbf{Short} — English \emph{bin}.) Which English word comes from the same root as \emph{bin}? (\textbf{Be}.) Next: the same verb for the person you are talking to.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[du bist]{du bist — \textquotedblleft{}you are\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:GE-C16-du-bist}



\begin{quote}
\emph{Du} is the familiar \textquotedblleft{}you\textquotedblright{} — the one for a friend. Its verb ending is \textbf{-st}, and for once \emph{sein} uses it.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: du bist}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{du bist} — \textquotedblleft{}you are.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

Take \emph{bin}, drop the \emph{n}, add the familiar \textbf{-st}: \emph{bi-} plus \emph{-st} is \emph{bist}. That is the same ending as \emph{du gehst}, \emph{du heißt}, \emph{du siehst}.

Of the six present forms of \emph{sein}, this is the only one that can be derived from another one. Enjoy it; it does not happen again.

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{u-long} — \emph{du} has a long, rounded \textbf{oo}, the vowel of English \emph{do}, held.
  \item \texttt{final-t} — German releases a final \textbf{t} fully and audibly. \emph{Bist} ends with a small puff of air; English tends to swallow it.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}du bist\textquotedblright{} — long \emph{u}, crisp final \emph{t}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}ich bin … du bist\textquotedblright{} — the pair
  \item \textquotedblleft{}du bist Peter.\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}ich bin, du bist.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}you are,\textquotedblright{} to a friend. (\textbf{Du bist}.) Which ending is that? (\textbf{-st}, the familiar one.) Which form is \emph{bist} built on? (\emph{\textbf{Bin}}.) Is the final \emph{t} released or swallowed? (\textbf{Released}.) Next: the form for everybody else.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[er ist]{er ist — \textquotedblleft{}he is\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:GE-C16-er-ist}



\begin{quote}
\emph{Bin} and \emph{bist} both start with \emph{b}. The third form does not, and it is the one you will hear most.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: er ist}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{er ist} — \textquotedblleft{}he is.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\textbf{er} is \textquotedblleft{}he.\textquotedblright{} The same \textbf{ist} serves three more subjects without changing at all: \textbf{sie ist} (\textquotedblleft{}she is\textquotedblright{}), \textbf{es ist} (\textquotedblleft{}it is\textquotedblright{}), and \textbf{das ist} (\textquotedblleft{}that is\textquotedblright{}) — \emph{es} and \emph{das} both already yours.

So one two-letter word covers everything that is not \emph{ich} and not \emph{du}, in the singular. It is the workhorse of the whole verb.

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{r-final} — the \emph{r} at the end of \emph{er} is not a full English \emph{r}. It softens towards a vowel, close to \emph{air} said without the tongue curling.
  \item \texttt{final-t} — \emph{ist} ends in the same released \textbf{t} as \emph{bist}.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{Ist} is the one form of \emph{sein} whose relatives you can name on sight:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{language} & \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}is\textquotedblright{}} \\
\midrule
German & \textbf{ist} \\
English & \textbf{is} \\
Latin & \emph{est} \\
French & \emph{est} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

All from Proto-Indo-European \textbf{*\emph{h\textsubscript{1}es-}}, \textquotedblleft{}to be\textquotedblright{} — and the infinitive \textbf{sein} is built on that root too. So \emph{sein} and \emph{ist} really do belong to each other; it is \emph{bin} and \emph{bist} that came from somewhere else.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}er ist, sie ist, es ist\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Das ist gut.\textquotedblright{} — \textquotedblleft{}that is good\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}ich bin, du bist, er ist\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}Das ist gut.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}he is.\textquotedblright{} (\textbf{Er ist}.) Which other subjects take the same form? (\emph{\textbf{Sie}}, \emph{\textbf{es}}, \emph{\textbf{das}}.) Say \textquotedblleft{}that is good.\textquotedblright{} (\textbf{Das ist gut}.) Which Latin word is \emph{ist}? (\emph{\textbf{Est}}.) Next: the form for more than one.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[wir sind]{wir sind — \textquotedblleft{}we are\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:GE-C16-wir-sind}



\begin{quote}
Three singular forms down. The plural starts here, and after \emph{bin}, \emph{bist}, \emph{ist}, this one will finally look like the verb it belongs to.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: wir sind}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{wir sind} — \textquotedblleft{}we are.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\textbf{wir} is \textquotedblleft{}we.\textquotedblright{} And \textbf{sind} shares its first two letters with the infinitive \emph{sein}, which is the first visible family resemblance in this verb.

Its Latin twin is \emph{sunt}, \textquotedblleft{}they are\textquotedblright{} — same \textbf{s}, same \textbf{n}, same closing stop, the same root wearing a different vowel.

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{w-as-v} — German \textbf{w} is English \textbf{v}. \emph{Wir} begins like \emph{veer}.
  \item \texttt{ie-long-ee} — \textbf{ie} is a long \textbf{ee}. \emph{Wir} is \emph{veer}, not \emph{wire}.
  \item \texttt{d-t-final} — the \textbf{d} at the end of \emph{sind} is spoken as a \textbf{t}, the same final devoicing you met on \emph{und}. Say \emph{zint}.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}wir sind\textquotedblright{} — \emph{veer zint}, final \emph{d} as \emph{t}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}wir sind gut.\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}sein … sind\textquotedblright{} — the family resemblance
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}wir sind, wir sind.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}we are.\textquotedblright{} (\textbf{Wir sind}.) How is the final \emph{d} pronounced? (As a \textbf{t}.) How does \emph{wir} begin? (Like English \textbf{v}.) Which Latin word is \emph{sind}? (\emph{\textbf{Sunt}}.) Next: the plural \textquotedblleft{}you.\textquotedblright{}
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ihr seid]{ihr seid — \textquotedblleft{}you are,\textquotedblright{} to several people}

\label{lesson:GE-C16-ihr-seid}



\begin{quote}
\emph{Du} is one friend. For two or more friends German has a separate word, and English used to have one as well.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: ihr seid}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{ihr seid} — \textquotedblleft{}you are,\textquotedblright{} said to more than one person you would each call \emph{du}.
\end{quote}

\textbf{ihr} is the familiar plural \textquotedblleft{}you\textquotedblright{} — a crowd of friends, a group of children, your own family. English once had \emph{ye} here and let it go, which is why one English \emph{you} now does the work of four German words.

\textbf{seid} opens exactly like the infinitive: \emph{sei-} is \emph{sein} without its \emph{n}. Both the \emph{s} and the \emph{ei} behave as they did there.

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{ie-long-ee} — \emph{ihr} is \emph{eer}, one long vowel; the \emph{h} only stretches it.
  \item \texttt{s-voiced} — \emph{seid} opens with the buzzing \textbf{z} of \emph{sein}.
  \item \texttt{diphthong-ei} — and carries the \emph{eye} vowel through. Say \emph{zite}.
\end{itemize}

\emph{Wir sind} and \emph{ihr seid} are the two plural forms, and they sound nothing alike, which makes them easy to keep apart.
\end{sounds}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}ihr seid\textquotedblright{} — \emph{eer zite}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}wir sind … ihr seid\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}sein … seid\textquotedblright{} — the same opening
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}ihr seid, ihr seid.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}you are\textquotedblright{} to a group of friends. (\textbf{Ihr seid}.) Which English word did that job before English dropped it? (\emph{\textbf{Ye}}.) Which part of \emph{seid} comes straight out of \emph{sein}? (\textbf{sei-}.) Next: the last form, and the one that does double duty.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[sie sind / Sie sind]{sie sind / Sie sind — \textquotedblleft{}they are,\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}you are,\textquotedblright{} politely}

\label{lesson:GE-C16-sie-sind}



\begin{quote}
The polite \textbf{Sie} is literally the word for \textquotedblleft{}they,\textquotedblright{} worn as a courtesy. Its verb form follows from that, and costs you nothing new.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: sie sind and Sie sind}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{sie sind} — \textquotedblleft{}they are.\textquotedblright{} \textbf{Sie sind} — \textquotedblleft{}you are,\textquotedblright{} to someone you would address formally.
\end{quote}

The form is \textbf{sind}, the very same word you learned for \emph{wir}. Nothing changes in the mouth at all: \emph{wir sind}, \emph{sie sind}, \emph{Sie sind} are three subjects and one verb form.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the capital carries the politeness}]
On the page, \emph{sie} and \emph{Sie} differ by exactly one capital letter — and German already spends capitals on grammar rather than decoration. In speech there is no difference at all; the context tells you which one is meant.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{written} & \textbf{means} \\
\midrule
\emph{sie sind} & they are \\
\emph{Sie sind} & you are, formally \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

That is the whole of it. Six subjects, and you have now met every present form of the verb.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}sie sind\textquotedblright{} — \textquotedblleft{}they are\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Sie sind Herr Peter Schmidt?\textquotedblright{} — politely
  \item \textquotedblleft{}wir sind, sie sind, Sie sind\textquotedblright{} — one form, three subjects
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}sie sind, Sie sind.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}they are.\textquotedblright{} (\textbf{Sie sind}.) Say \textquotedblleft{}you are\textquotedblright{} to a stranger. (\textbf{Sie sind} — same sound.) What separates the two on paper? (\textbf{The capital S}.) How many different present forms of this verb have you now met? (\textbf{Five} — \emph{bin, bist, ist, sind, seid}.) Next: one adjective, so you can finally say something about yourself.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[müde]{müde — \textquotedblleft{}tired\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:GE-C16-muede}



\begin{quote}
\emph{Ich bin} is a sentence waiting for one more word. Here is the word that finishes it most often.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: müde}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{müde} — \textquotedblleft{}tired.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Ich bin müde.} — \textquotedblleft{}I am tired.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

Two syllables, stress on the first: \emph{mü-duh}. It is an adjective, and after \emph{sein} an adjective takes \textbf{no ending at all} — the same bare form serves every subject. \emph{Ich bin müde}, \emph{du bist müde}, \emph{wir sind müde}.

That is worth noticing, because German adjectives are famous for their endings. They only take them in front of a noun. Standing after \emph{sein}, they stand still.

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{umlaut-ue} — \textbf{ü} is the vowel you make by rounding your lips for \emph{oo} and then saying \emph{ee} without moving them. The dots are the fronting mark you already know: the mouth shifts forward, the lips stay round.
\end{itemize}

The final \textbf{-e} is a soft \emph{uh}, never silent. \emph{mü-duh}, two beats, the weight on the first.
\end{sounds}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}müde\textquotedblright{} — round the lips, say \emph{ee}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Ich bin müde.\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Er ist müde. Wir sind müde.\textquotedblright{} — the adjective never changes
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}Ich bin müde.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}I am tired.\textquotedblright{} (\textbf{Ich bin müde}.) How do you make the \textbf{ü}? (\textbf{Round for \emph{oo}, say \emph{ee}.}) Does \emph{müde} change after \emph{sein}? (\textbf{No} — no ending.) Say \textquotedblleft{}we are tired.\textquotedblright{} (\textbf{Wir sind müde}.) Next: everything at once, on purpose.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Practice — the whole present of sein}

\label{lesson:GE-C16-praesens-practice}



\begin{quote}
No new words. Every form below has had its own lesson, so this is the first time it is safe to put them all on one page — as a recap, not as something to memorise from cold.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the six forms, assembled}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{singular} & \textbf{plural} \\
\midrule
ich \textbf{bin} & wir \textbf{sind} \\
du \textbf{bist} & ihr \textbf{seid} \\
er/sie/es \textbf{ist} & sie/Sie \textbf{sind} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Six subjects, five different forms — \emph{sind} does double duty. Look at that with fresh eyes now that you can say all of it: \emph{bin} and \emph{ist} do not look like forms of the same word, and the next chapter explains why they aren't.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{The exchange}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{German} & \textbf{English} \\
\midrule
\emph{Hallo! Wie geht es dir?} & Hello! How are you? \\
\emph{Danke, ich bin müde.} & Thanks — I am tired. \\
\emph{Du bist müde? Ich auch.} & You are tired? Me too. \\
\emph{Dann sind wir müde. Aber das ist gut.} & Then we are tired. But that is good. \\
\emph{Bis morgen!} & See you tomorrow! \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Three small joining words slip in there without needing lessons of their own, because each can be read straight off the translation: \textbf{auch} (\textquotedblleft{}too\textquotedblright{}), \textbf{dann} (\textquotedblleft{}then\textquotedblright{}) and \textbf{aber} (\textquotedblleft{}but\textquotedblright{}).

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the six in order — \textquotedblleft{}ich bin, du bist, er ist, wir sind, ihr seid, sie sind\textquotedblright{}
  \item the same six backwards
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Ich bin müde.\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}Du bist müde.\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}Wir sind müde.\textquotedblright{}
  \item the whole exchange, both voices
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}ich bin, du bist, er ist, wir sind, ihr seid, sie sind.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Run the six forms without looking. Which one form covers \emph{wir}, \emph{sie} and \emph{Sie}? (\emph{\textbf{Sind}}.) Which is the only form built out of another one? (\emph{\textbf{Bist}}, from \emph{bin}.) Say \textquotedblleft{}that is good.\textquotedblright{} (\textbf{Das ist gut}.) Say \textquotedblleft{}you are tired\textquotedblright{} to a group. (\textbf{Ihr seid müde}.) Next: where these forms came from — three different verbs, none of them each other.
\end{tcolorbox}
